passage:
Team lead's note, Thursday

Tushar asked to speak to me privately this morning. He has been late four times this month and I had assumed it was traffic. He said it was not. He told me his drinking had crept up from weekends to most nights, that he kept promising himself to stop after the quarter and kept breaking it, and that his partner was worried. His hands were shaking a little as he spoke, but he said he wanted to fix it before it got worse.
I thanked him for trusting me and said this took courage. I gave him the number for our employee counselling line and suggested he also see his own doctor. We agreed on flexible mornings for now while he gets support. I will check in with him on Monday. 

Minakshi

qa.q: How many times had Tushar been late this month?
qa.a: He had been late four times this month.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he spoke to Minakshi, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was nervous and probably ashamed, since his hands were shaking a little, but he also felt determined to fix it before it got worse.

qa.q: How did Minakshi support Tushar well after he spoke up?
qa.a: Minakshi thanked him, called it courage, gave him the counselling number, suggested his doctor, arranged flexible mornings and planned a check-in.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see Tushar's decision to speak up?
qa.a: Minakshi sees it as courage rather than failure, and responds with support instead of judging the late mornings.

grounding: It shows a person noticing that use is rising and promises are broken, and reaching out to a trusted person who points to a counsellor and a doctor.

passage:
Tuesday night

Okay, writing this down so I can't pretend later.
I said I'd only vape at parties. Then only after work. Today I went through a whole pod before lunch and snapped at a customer because the craving hit mid-call.
I've made the "last one" promise maybe ten times since Diwali.
So tonight I called Gopika. She's my cousin but also the one person who never makes me feel stupid. I cried a bit. She didn't lecture, just said, "You noticed. That's the hard part. Now let someone help."
I booked a clinic appointment for Friday and wrote down everything I want to tell the doctor, before I lose my nerve.
Weirdly, I feel lighter. Not fixed. Lighter.

Maria

qa.q: Whom did Maria call tonight?
qa.a: Maria called Gopika, Maria's cousin.

qa.q: How does Maria feel after booking the appointment?
qa.a: Maria feels lighter and a little relieved, while knowing it is not fixed yet.

qa.q: Which choice in the entry was the real turning point, and why?
qa.a: Calling Gopika and booking the clinic, because Maria stopped relying on broken promises and let other people help.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Maria's call?
qa.a: Gopika likely sees it as a brave step rather than a failure, which is why she says the hard part is noticing.

grounding: It shows someone realising cravings are strong and promises to cut down keep breaking, and reaching out to a trusted person and a doctor.

subtopic: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances
passage: In the small town of Bhadohi, Abhinav had chewed tobacco since college. It used to be one packet a day. Now it was four, and he woke with cravings before he'd even opened his eyes. His gums bled. His mother had cried twice and made him promise to stop; he'd lasted three days each time, then hidden the packets in his scooter. One evening, spitting red into the drain, he felt a jolt of fear. He told his friend Wasim, 'I can't stop on my own.' Wasim didn't laugh. 'The district hospital has a clinic for this. My uncle went.' The next morning they rode there together. Sitting on the bench outside the doctor's room, Abhinav felt ashamed. Wasim nudged him. 'Asking takes more guts than chewing, yaar.' Abhinav went in.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav hide the packets?
qa.a: In his scooter.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel sitting outside the doctor's room?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, even while taking a brave step.

qa.q: What signs told Abhinav it was time to get help?
qa.a: Rising use, strong morning cravings, bleeding gums and broken promises to his mother.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's mother feel when she hears he went to the clinic?
qa.a: She will likely feel relieved and hopeful after the tears and broken promises.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising rising tobacco use, strong cravings and broken promises, and reaching out through a trusted friend to a doctor.

subtopic: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances
passage: Marek had smoked cannabis on weekends since university. In the past year in Kraków it had crept into weeknights, then most evenings. He'd told himself and his girlfriend Rania, twice, that he'd cut down. Both times he'd lasted less than a week. He'd been late to work four times this month, and his manager had noticed. One Sunday, looking at his empty bank app and the full ashtray, he finally said it out loud. 'Rania, I think I need help. I can't seem to stop.' She put her tea down and took his hand. 'I'm proud of you for saying it.' On Monday he rang his doctor's surgery and booked an appointment. Rania found a local support line too. Marek felt scared, but lighter than he had in months.

qa.q: How many times had Marek been late to work this month?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling after admitting he needed help?
qa.a: He felt scared but lighter than he had in months.

qa.q: Which step showed Marek recognising the problem?
qa.a: Admitting out loud to Rania that he could not stop, after broken promises and trouble at work.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt hearing him admit it?
qa.a: She felt proud of him and probably relieved that he was ready to get help.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing rising use, broken promises and harm to work, and reaching out to a doctor and a trusted person as a sign of strength.

passage:
The clinic waiting room had a fan that clicked on every turn. Gurpreet held the token slip, number 14, and read it again.
"You can still leave," Kunal said quietly beside him.
"I'm not leaving." Gurpreet stared at the floor. "Three times I said I'd only drink on Saturdays. Three times I broke it by Tuesday. Last month I missed my daughter Harleen's parent-teacher meeting because I was asleep on the sofa." He rubbed his face. "At night I think about it all the time. That's not a choice anymore."
"Coming here is the bravest thing I've seen you do," Kunal said.
The display flashed 14. Gurpreet stood, knees unsteady, and walked in to see the doctor.

qa.q: What token number did Gurpreet hold?
qa.a: Number 14.

qa.q: Why were Gurpreet's knees unsteady when the display flashed 14?
qa.a: He was nervous and ashamed, yet determined; telling a doctor felt huge, but he had already decided not to leave.

qa.q: Which signs told Gurpreet it was time to get help?
qa.a: Broken promises to cut down, constant thoughts about drinking at night, and missing his daughter's school meeting.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Gurpreet's visit to the clinic?
qa.a: Kunal sees it as strength, not failure, and calls it the bravest thing Gurpreet has done.

grounding: Shows a person recognising broken promises, strong cravings and a suffering family life, and reaching out to a doctor as an act of strength.
